  "text": "On his last afternoon at the hardware shop, Martin counted the brass hinges twice. There were seventeen, though the stock book said eighteen.

He wrote seventeen in pencil.

The new owner was coming at four. She had asked him to leave the keys, the supplier numbers and instructions for the till. He had put everything in an envelope except the instructions. The till opened if you pressed firmly above the drawer. He couldn't think how to explain how firmly.

At quarter to four, a boy came in with a cupboard handle.

“Have you got one like this?”

Martin turned it over. Cream plastic, split around the screw hole.

“Not for years.”

The boy took it back.

“It's our landlord's cupboard.”

Martin looked at the clock, then fetched the biscuit tin from beneath the counter. Inside were washers, odd knobs and fittings he had kept whenever someone said to throw them away.

They emptied it onto a sheet of newspaper.

The new owner arrived while they were sorting.

“Sorry,” Martin said. “Nearly finished.”

She set her bag down and picked up the broken handle.

“My gran had these.”

Near the bottom they found a brown one with the same spacing between the holes.

“Will that do?” Martin asked.

The boy considered it.

“If I change the other one too.”

The new owner pulled up a stool.

“There might be another.”

Martin moved the newspaper towards her. Then he took the keys from his pocket and laid them beside the till.

He stayed long enough to find the second handle."
